local_facts.title: Florida caps a dryer duct at 35 feet, and fittings count
local_facts.claim: Section M1502 of the 2023 Florida Building Code, Residential, requires dryer exhaust ducts to terminate outside the building with a backdraft damper and forbids screens at the termination. The duct must be metal with a smooth interior, 4 inches nominal, and may not be joined with screws. Its maximum length is 35 feet from the transition duct connection to the outlet, reduced by fittings: 5 feet for each 4-inch-radius mitered 90-degree elbow and 2 feet 6 inches for each mitered 45. The flexible transition duct may be no longer than 8 feet and may not be concealed in construction.
local_facts.why_it_matters: A single-story Ocala house with the laundry in the middle of the floor plan often sends its dryer duct up through the attic and out the roof. Two or three elbows on that route eat ten or fifteen feet of the allowance, and a long, bent run is exactly where lint settles. The length rule is the first thing to measure when clothes take two cycles.

local_facts.title: About one Marion County home in six is a mobile home
local_facts.claim: The Census Bureau's American Community Survey 2024 one-year estimates count 199,453 housing units in Marion County, of which 35,391 are mobile homes and 138,141 are single-family detached houses. Federal manufactured home standards at 24 CFR 3280.708 require clothes dryers to exhaust to the outside through a moisture and lint exhaust duct, state that the duct shall not terminate beneath the manufactured home, and prohibit screws or other fasteners that project into the duct.
local_facts.why_it_matters: A dryer duct that ends under the floor instead of past the skirting dumps hot, wet, lint-laden air into the crawl space, where it collects on the underside of the home. In a county with this many manufactured homes, checking where the duct actually ends is part of every cleaning.

local_facts.title: Three in ten residents are 65 or older
local_facts.claim: The Florida Office of Economic and Demographic Research county profile puts 29.8 percent of Marion County residents at age 65 and over, against 21.2 percent statewide, with a median age of 50.3 against 43.0 for Florida. The county's population was 375,908 at the 2020 Census and is estimated at 433,765 for 2025.
local_facts.why_it_matters: Pulling a dryer away from the wall, working on a roof cap, or climbing a ladder to an eave are the parts of vent maintenance most likely to end in a fall. In a county this old, a vent cleaning is often a job handed off rather than one done on a Saturday afternoon, and the cleaning should leave the outlet easy to check from the ground.

local_facts.title: More horses than any other county in the country
local_facts.claim: The 2023 equine economic impact study released in February 2024 by the Florida Thoroughbred Breeders' and Owners' Association counts about 75,000 horses and ponies in Marion County, more than any other single county or parish in the United States, with roughly 210,000 acres, over a fifth of the county's land, in horse-related use and about 28,500 equine and equine-related jobs.
local_facts.why_it_matters: Farm households and barn workers wash saddle pads, barn towels and work clothes that come in coated in hair, hay chaff and arena dust. Much of that slips past a lint screen and settles in the duct, so a farm or barn laundry clogs its vent faster than a suburban one and should be checked more often.
